impelled

/im-PELD/ - rhymes with spelled · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Impelled means driven or urged from within to take action.

After the museum fire, Teo felt impelled to photograph every remaining mural in the city.

Example

Reading her grandmother's unfinished field diary, Lena felt impelled to complete the bird count herself, and was out on the marsh by Saturday.

Impelled is the past form of impel, and it nearly always appears in one shape: someone is impelled — or feels impelled — to do something. The push comes from inside, stirred by feeling or circumstance; forced and compelled name pressure applied from outside.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

driven: Driven means pushed toward an act by any pressure at all — ambition, a boss, a deadline — whether it starts inside you or out. Impelled is narrower: the push is felt within, stirred by feeling or circumstance, in the frame 'felt impelled to.'

moved: Moved means stirred by emotion — a film can leave you moved without your doing anything about it. Impelled goes the extra step: the stirring becomes action, and the person impelled to write the letter actually reaches for the pen.

obliged: Obliged means bound by duty, rules, or politeness — you thank the host because you should. Impelled works from inside instead: no rule requires the act; an inner push, not an obligation, sets the impelled person moving.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deterred: pushed away from acting by fear or doubt

unwilling: holding back from the act instead of being carried toward it

Where it sits · how much choice the push leaves — tempted → impelled → forced

tempted vs. impelled: Being tempted is milder — the idea merely looks attractive — and it stops short of impelled, where the push has real force behind it.

forced vs. impelled: Forced goes further than impelled: an impelled volunteer still chooses to act, while a forced one has had the choice taken away.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: in, into, against (a form of in-)

Root — -pell-

Root — -pell-: to push, to drive (Latin pellere)

Suffix — -ed

Suffix — -ed: past — the push already delivered

Put it together

Put it together: The im- here is the directional in- — 'into, against' — not the negative one: im- + pellere ('to drive') + -ed gives 'driven into action.' Impelled looks as if it could mean 'not pelled,' but there is no 'pelled' to negate; the word is all push.

Use the root in a new word: compel

Use the root in a new word: compel: The subpoena compelled the accountant to hand over every ledger by Friday.

Word Choice

formal

Impelled is the past of impel — see that card — and nearly always travels in the frame 'felt impelled to.' Reach for it when an inner push, not outside force, sets someone acting; when the choice is taken away entirely, English switches to compelled.
